convention: literal line-by-line, as in batch H06's brief
reasoning_summary:
2.11.11-12 aeternis ... consiliis read as ablative of means, also felt with minorem (comparison), and noted; 2.11.15 and 24 have accusatives of respect (canos odorati capillos, comam religata), kept as 'as to' with notes.
2.12.21 num rendered 'surely you would not', with a note that nothing is added to the negative; 2.12.27 quae = the kisses, poscente as ablative of comparison, eripi passive; Licymnia's possible identity noted.
2.13.19 robur kept as 'oak' (strength, perhaps the Tullianum) with a note; 2.13.29-32 utrumque/digna/volgus construction kept on its lines with agreement notes, volgus kept as subject of bibit.
2.14.5-9 trecenis = three hundred each day; unda (Styx) as the subject of enaviganda; 2.14.22-24 neque ... ulla kept split across lines, not resolved.
2.15.4 caelebs platanus kept as 'unwedded plane-tree' (the vine metaphor) with a note; 2.15.16 arcton as 'the North' (the Bear), noted.
2.16.7-8 ve-/nale divided across the line end as in the Latin, the English divided the same way ('pur-/chasable'); 2.16.10 submovet lictor kept with its crowd-clearing sense noted.
2.17.4 mearum ... rerum hyperbaton kept, so line 4 reads 'pillar, affairs'; 2.17.14 Gyas kept as in the source (also Gyges), noted; 2.17.28 sustulerat pluperfect indicative in an unreal condition, noted.
Supplied possessives (her, his, my, its) are flagged in notes throughout; verb-before-subject lines rephrased so no subject and object flip in English.
